z-m-23-01.title: x⁴ + x² − 6 = 0: checking the solution that says there are four real roots
z-m-23-01.topic: Judging the number of real roots of a quartic equation in the form of a quadratic in x²
z-m-23-01.goal: In a quartic equation solved by letting x² be a new letter, check the range in which the new letter's value can give a real x to find the error in the solution, and explain the conditions under which the signs of the coefficients alone settle the number of real roots.
z-m-23-01.material: Yeongseo solved the quartic equation x⁴ + x² − 6 = 0 to find all its real solutions (real roots). Here, real roots means only the solutions that are real numbers, and imaginary solutions are not counted. (x⁴ is read as "x to the fourth power" and x² is read as "x squared".)
z-m-23-01.thinking.0: Finding the error in a solution
z-m-23-01.thinking.2: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-23-01.prereq.0: H1 in this task only marks the difficulty of this production category; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to high school grade 1. Assumed learning order: learners who have already learned quadratic equations, quadratic inequalities, and the relationship between roots and coefficients.
z-m-23-01.prereq.1: Practice solving by factoring a quadratic expression in x²
z-m-23-01.prereq.2: Judging signs using the sum and product of the two roots of a quadratic equation
z-m-23-01.prereq.3: Telling real and imaginary numbers apart (no real number gives a negative value when squared)
z-m-23-01.s.s1.prompt: Which line in Yeongseo's solution is the first wrong one? Choose one line. (Errors that follow from it are explained together in the explanation.)
z-m-23-01.s.s1.hint.0: Plug the value from each line directly into the original equation x⁴ + x² − 6 and check one by one whether it becomes 0.
z-m-23-01.s.s1.hint.1: Think about the range of values that x² in the place of t can take for a real x, and compare line 3 and line 4.
z-m-23-01.s.s1.line.0: Letting x² be t gives t² + t − 6 = 0.
z-m-23-01.s.s1.line.3: From x² = −3, x = ±√3, and from x² = 2, x = ±√2.
z-m-23-01.s.s1.line.4: Therefore there are four real roots: −√3, −√2, √2, √3.
z-m-23-01.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is the first wrong one. A real number x is at least 0 when squared, so there is no real x with x² = −3. So ±√3 are not real roots (if you plug x = √3 into the original equation, 9 + 3 − 6 = 6 ≠ 0). The "four" in line 5 is also wrong because of this, and the real roots are the two, −√2 and √2. Lines 1 to 3 are correct.
z-m-23-01.s.s2.prompt: For integers p and q, in x⁴ + px² + q = 0, if you only know that q < 0 and do not know p, how many different real roots are there?
z-m-23-01.s.s2.hint.0: Count and compare the real roots directly in the three equations where q is the same −4 and p is −5, 0, 3.
z-m-23-01.s.s2.hint.1: Write as an equation how the product of the two roots of the quadratic equation in t=x² relates to q, and check the sign.
z-m-23-01.s.s2.o.a: 4: each of the two values of x² gives two real x
z-m-23-01.s.s2.r.a: A value where x² is negative gives no real x. First look at the sign of the values x² can take.
z-m-23-01.s.s2.o.b: 2: only one of the values of x² gives real x
z-m-23-01.s.s2.r.b: This judgment works out what signs the two values of x² have.
z-m-23-01.s.s2.o.c: 0: x⁴ and x² are at least 0, so their sum cannot be 0
z-m-23-01.s.s2.r.c: If you plug in x = 0, the value of the expression is q, which is negative. Look at the change of sign to see whether there is a place where the value of the expression is 0.
z-m-23-01.s.s2.o.d: Cannot be known: depending on the value of p, it is one of 0, 2, or 4
z-m-23-01.s.s2.r.d: This judgment thinks the value of p is needed. But first check whether there is a fact that is fixed by q < 0 alone regardless of p.
z-m-23-01.s.s2.explain: The product of the two roots of t² + pt + q = 0 with t = x² is q < 0, so one root is positive and the other is negative (the discriminant p² − 4q is also always positive). Only a positive t gives two real x, so whatever p is, there are 2 different real roots.
z-m-23-01.s.s3.prompt: Explain, using the sign of t (= x²), why there are 2 real roots regardless of p when q < 0, and give one example in numbers where the number of real roots depends on p when q > 0.
z-m-23-01.s.s3.hint.0: First write in one sentence the fact that the product of the two roots of t is q and the sign of q.
z-m-23-01.s.s3.hint.1: As examples of q > 0, solve p = −5, q = 4 and p = 1, q = 1 and count the real roots, then write one of them.
z-m-23-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If q < 0, the product of the two roots of t is ... so ...
z-m-23-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you use the fact that the two roots of t have different signs when q < 0 as the reason?
z-m-23-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write the connection "only a positive t gives real x"?
z-m-23-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you solve the q > 0 example you gave yourself and check the number of real roots?
z-m-23-01.s.s3.model.0: q is the product of the two roots of t²+pt+q=0 and it is negative, so one t is positive and one is negative. From x²=positive there are two real x, and from x²=negative there is no real x, so there are always 2 real roots. If q>0, x⁴−5x²+4=0 has t=1, 4, so 4 real roots, but x⁴+x²+1=0 has no real roots.
z-m-23-01.s.s3.model.1: If you let t=x², the product of the two roots is negative, so their signs are different. A negative t cannot come from a square, so only the two x from the positive t are real roots. Even when q is positive, it depends on p: with p=−2, q=1 there are 2 real roots, and with p=3, q=2 there are 0 real roots.

z-m-23-02.title: If one root is 1 + i, is the other root fixed?
z-m-23-02.topic: Conditions needed to fix the other root in a quadratic equation with an imaginary root
z-m-23-02.goal: Tell apart the information that is needed and the information that is lacking for fixing the other root when one root is imaginary, and make your own counterexamples where the coefficients may not be real.
z-m-23-02.material: One root of the quadratic equation x² + px + q = 0 is 1 + i. (i is the number whose square is −1 and is read as "eye".) Mina said, "The other root is 1 − i," and Doyun said, "That alone cannot fix the other root." It has not yet been said what kind of numbers p and q are.
z-m-23-02.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-23-02.thinking.2: Explaining why a condition is needed
z-m-23-02.prereq.0: H1 in this task only marks the difficulty of this production category; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to high school grade 1. Assumed learning order: learners who have already learned quadratic equations, quadratic inequalities, and the relationship between roots and coefficients.
z-m-23-02.prereq.1: Addition and multiplication of complex numbers, the real part and the imaginary part
z-m-23-02.prereq.2: The relationship that the sum of the two roots of a quadratic equation is −p and the product is q
z-m-23-02.prereq.3: The meaning of the discriminant (the kinds of roots when the coefficients are real)
z-m-23-02.s.s1.prompt: Besides the fact that one root of the quadratic equation x² + px + q = 0 is 1 + i, what extra information would fix the other root to exactly one? Choose all the pieces of information that fix it that way.
z-m-23-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each option, look one by one with numbers for an example that satisfies this condition but has a different other root.
z-m-23-02.s.s1.hint.1: Use the relationship that the sum of the two roots is −p to write the other root directly for each option.
z-m-23-02.s.s1.o.a: The sum of the two roots is real
z-m-23-02.s.s1.r.a: The fact that the sum is real alone cannot narrow the other root down to one. Write the other root when the sum is 3 and when the sum is 2.
z-m-23-02.s.s1.o.b: p and q are both real
z-m-23-02.s.s1.r.b: This judgment knows how a condition on the coefficients limits the shape of the roots.
z-m-23-02.s.s1.r.c: From the discriminant being negative alone, you cannot tell whether the roots come in a pair. Calculate the discriminant for the case where the roots are 1 + i and 1.
z-m-23-02.s.s1.r.d: This judgment uses the relationship that the sum of the two roots is −p.
z-m-23-02.s.s1.explain: If p and q are real, an imaginary root comes in a pair with its conjugate complex number, so the other root is fixed as 1 − i. Even knowing the value of p fixes the other root because the sum is −p (if p = −3, then 3 − (1 + i) = 2 − i). The information that the sum is real is not enough, because the other root could be 1 − i or 2 − i. Even if the discriminant is negative, there is the case where the roots are 1 + i and 1 (p = −(2 + i), q = 1 + i, p² − 4q = −1), so it is not fixed.
z-m-23-02.s.s2.prompt: Writing the other root as m + ni (m and n are integers), make 3 different examples where p is real but q is not real. (The sum of the two roots is −p and the product is q. i is the number whose square is −1.)
z-m-23-02.s.s2.hint.0: First write what value the imaginary part of the sum of the two roots (1 + i) + (m + ni) must be for p to be real.
z-m-23-02.s.s2.hint.1: With the n that satisfies the imaginary-part condition, expand the product (1 + i)(m + ni), find the m that makes the imaginary part 0, and avoid that m.
z-m-23-02.s.s2.var.m: The real part m of the other root
z-m-23-02.s.s2.var.n: The imaginary part n of the other root
z-m-23-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Please take m and n to be integers.
z-m-23-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum of the two roots is real (p is real).
z-m-23-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of the two roots (1 + m) + (1 + n)i is not real. p is not real either.
z-m-23-02.s.s2.ok.c3: The imaginary part of the product of the two roots is not 0, so q is not real.
z-m-23-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The imaginary part of the product of the two roots (m − n) + (m + n)i is 0, so q is real.
z-m-23-02.s.s2.explain: For the sum to be real, the imaginary part 1 + n must be 0, so n = −1. Then the product is (m + 1) + (m − 1)i, so if m ≠ 1, q is not real. Example: if the other root is 2 − i, then p = −3 (real) and q = (1 + i)(2 − i) = 3 + i (not real). If m = 1, the other root is 1 − i and q = 2, which is real.
z-m-23-02.s.s3.prompt: Explain to a friend. What can you say about the other root of a quadratic equation with one root 1 + i, when there is the statement "the coefficients p and q are real" and when there is not?
z-m-23-02.s.s3.hint.0: First write in one sentence the other root when there is the condition that the coefficients are real.
z-m-23-02.s.s3.hint.1: When there is no condition, recall the example you made earlier (2 − i and so on) and write in one sentence that the other root is not just one possibility.
z-m-23-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If p and q are real, ... If there is no such statement, ...
z-m-23-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the other root specifically when the coefficients are real?
z-m-23-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Do you know at least one example (for example, 2 − i or 1) that can be the other root when there is no condition?
z-m-23-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you connect in your own words why the condition "the coefficients are real" is needed?
z-m-23-02.s.s3.model.0: If p and q are real, an imaginary root comes in a pair with its conjugate, so the other root is 1−i. If there is no such statement, there are several possibilities like 2−i or 1, so the other root cannot be fixed.
z-m-23-02.s.s3.model.1: If the coefficients are real, the conjugate complex number 1−i of 1+i is the other root. If there is no condition on the coefficients, it can change, like 2−i if the sum is 3 and 1−i if the sum is 2, so we cannot say it is one value.
z-m-23-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: It gave concrete examples that change with the sum.

z-m-23-03.title: When is the thrown ball low, at 6 m or below?
z-m-23-03.topic: Applying quadratic inequalities: considering the range of the variable too
z-m-23-03.goal: In a situation modeled by a quadratic inequality, do not carry the solution of the expression over as the answer as it is, but interpret it together with the range where the model is valid, and make values that fit the conditions yourself.
z-m-23-03.material: A ball was thrown upward from a height of 1 m above the ground. The height t seconds after the throw is given by h(t) = −5t² + 20t + 1 (unit: m), and this expression can be used only while the ball is flying (from the moment of the throw to the moment it touches the ground). Ignore air resistance.
z-m-23-03.thinking.0: Revising your expectation by going back and forth between the table and the expression
z-m-23-03.thinking.2: Making values that fit the conditions
z-m-23-03.prereq.0: H1 in this task only marks the difficulty of this production category; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to high school grade 1. Assumed learning order: learners who have already learned quadratic equations, quadratic inequalities, and the relationship between roots and coefficients.
z-m-23-03.prereq.1: Solving quadratic inequalities and reading the inequality signs of the solution
z-m-23-03.prereq.2: Calculating by plugging function values into an expression
z-m-23-03.s.s1.prompt: You want to find out when the height of the thrown ball is low, at 6 m or below. Look at how your judgment changes each time a piece of information is revealed.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.hint.0: Compare the height at each time in the table with 6 m and mark which rows are 6 m or below.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.hint.1: Plug the times that are not in the table (0.5 s, 3.5 s) into the expression and check whether the height is 6 m or below.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.0.info:
A ball was thrown upward from a height of 1 m above the ground. The height t seconds after the throw is h(t) = −5t² + 20t + 1 (unit m), and this expression can be used only while the ball is flying (from the moment of the throw to the moment it touches the ground). The heights at some times are as follows.
t (s): 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
h (m): 1, 16, 21, 16, 1
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: When after the throw is the height 6 m or below? Look at the table and make a prediction first.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.0.after: Looking at the table, the height is low at 1 m at 0 s and 4 s, and 16 m or more from 1 to 3 s. So it seems the low times are twice, near the start and near the end. But the table shows only whole seconds, so you need the expression to find out exactly where the boundaries are.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It seems to be two time periods, right after the throw and just before the ball falls
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This judgment sees that the height is low at the start (0 s) and near the end (4 s) in the table.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It seems to be only once, right after the throw (since it soon goes up)
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You missed the row with height 1 m at 4 s. Compare the last row of the table with 6 m.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It seems to be around 2 s, when the ball is highest
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: At 2 s the height is 21 m, the highest. Read again that the question asks for when the height is low.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: We cannot tell from whole seconds alone, so we need to solve the expression
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This judgment is aware of the limit that the table shows only whole seconds.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.1.info: Rearranging −5t² + 20t + 1 ≤ 6 gives t² − 4t + 1 ≥ 0. The values of t where this quadratic expression is 0 are 2 − √3 ≈ 0.27 and 2 + √3 ≈ 3.73. Looking at the expression alone, you get t ≤ 0.27 or t ≥ 3.73.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Can you write this result as the answer for the "low times" as it is?
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.1.after: At t = 0.2 and 3.8, the height is 4.8 m in both cases, so being 6 m or below is correct. But t ≥ 3.73 has no end, so it includes times after the ball has touched the ground. This expression can be used only while the ball is flying, so you need to consider the range of t.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Yes. The solution of the inequality came out, so it is the answer as it is
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This judgment only carried over the solution of the expression. Reread the first sentence of the information to see at which times this expression can be used.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: We need to check whether the range of t is limited to the time the ball is flying
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This judgment is aware of the range in which the expression can be used.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The solution is probably wrong. The table and the two time periods do not match
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The table (0 s and 4 s are low) and the result (near the start, near the end) actually match well. Approximate the values of the roots and compare them with the table.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: First compare roughly by plugging t = 0.2 and 3.8 into the expression to see whether the height is 6 m or below
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This judgment checks the result against the table and approximations.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.2.info: The time the ball touches the ground is when h(t) = 0. From −5t² + 20t + 1 = 0, t = 2 + √4.2 ≈ 4.05 (s). So the times when the ball is flying are 0 ≤ t ≤ 4.05.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: How is it appropriate to write the times when the "height is 6 m or below"?
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.2.after: The low times are 0 ≤ t ≤ 0.27 (about 0.27 s) and 3.73 ≤ t ≤ 4.05 (about 0.32 s). Together that is about 0.59 s, which is short.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The range of the time was not written. It can be read as the ball still existing after 4.05 s.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You read the solution of the quadratic inequality t² − 4t + 1 ≥ 0 as being between the two roots. Check against the fact that the height at 2 s is 21 m.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This judgment wrote the solution of the expression together with the range in which the ball is flying.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You approximated 4 s as the time it touches the ground. At 4 s the height is 1 m, so the ball is still flying.
z-m-23-03.s.s1.reflect: Your first prediction of "two time periods, near the start and near the end" held to the end. What changed were the exact values of the boundaries and the point that you must check the range the variable can take before carrying over the solution of an expression as it is. Look back at whether you checked the range in which the expression is used before you wrote the solution of the expression.
z-m-23-03.s.s2.prompt: Write three different times t (s) at which the height is 6 m or below and the ball is still flying. (You may write them as decimals.)
z-m-23-03.s.s2.hint.0: Plug one time right after the throw and one time just before the fall into the expression and calculate the heights.
z-m-23-03.s.s2.hint.1: If the height you calculated is greater than 6, move the time toward 0 or toward 4 and calculate again.
z-m-23-03.s.s2.var.t: The time t (s) after the throw
z-m-23-03.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a time after the throw.
z-m-23-03.s.s2.fail.c1: t must be after the moment of the throw (0 s).
z-m-23-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The ball has not yet touched the ground.
z-m-23-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The height is less than 0. It is a time after the ball has already touched the ground.
z-m-23-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The height is 6 m or below.
z-m-23-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The height is higher than 6 m. Plug it into the expression and calculate.
z-m-23-03.s.s2.explain: The low times are 0 ≤ t ≤ 0.27 or 3.73 ≤ t ≤ 4.05. For example, t = 0 (1 m), 0.2 (4.8 m), 3.8 (4.8 m), 4 (1 m) fit the conditions. t = 0.3 or 3.7 gives 6.55 m, which is over 6 m, and t = 5 gives a height of −24, below the ground, so the ball has already touched down.

z-m-23-04.title: Can a table of values settle the integer solutions of f(x) < 0?
z-m-23-04.topic: Judging the integer solutions of a quadratic inequality using a table of values and the sign of a quadratic function
z-m-23-04.goal: Judge the solution of a quadratic inequality from sign changes in a table of function values, sort out claims that cannot be made from the table alone, and explain which conditions settle the conclusion.
z-m-23-04.material:
The function f(x) = ax² + bx + c is a quadratic function whose x² coefficient a is positive, but we do not know the values of a, b, c. All we know is the table of values below, and all the x in the table are integers.
x: −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
f(x): 3, −1, −3, −3, −1, 3
Question: Which integers x satisfy f(x) < 0? (In the table, the upper row is x and the lower row is the value of f(x), and numbers in the same position are paired.)
z-m-23-04.thinking.0: Drawing a conclusion from a table (evidence)
z-m-23-04.thinking.1: Sorting out claims that cannot be made from the table
z-m-23-04.thinking.2: Explaining why a condition is needed
z-m-23-04.prereq.0: H1 in this task only marks the difficulty of this production category; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to high school grade 1. Assumed learning order: learners who have already learned quadratic equations, quadratic inequalities, and the relationship between roots and coefficients.
z-m-23-04.prereq.1: The shape of the graph of a quadratic function (the sign of a and the direction it opens)
z-m-23-04.prereq.2: The intersections of a quadratic function with the x-axis, and the axis of symmetry
z-m-23-04.prereq.3: Reading the solution of a quadratic inequality from a graph
z-m-23-04.s.s1.prompt: When using only the table and not finding the expression, which statement can be settled about the integers x that satisfy f(x) < 0?
z-m-23-04.s.s1.hint.0: In the table, mark between which x values f changes from positive to negative and from negative to positive.
z-m-23-04.s.s1.hint.1: Picture the shape of a quadratic function with a > 0, think about how many intervals the x with values less than 0 form, and compare with the integers outside the table.
z-m-23-04.s.s1.o.a: Only the two, 1 and 2. They are where the value is smallest in the table
z-m-23-04.s.s1.r.a: This judgment looks only at where the value is smallest. f(x) < 0 means all x with values less than 0.
z-m-23-04.s.s1.o.b: All six integers in the table, from −1 to 4
z-m-23-04.s.s1.r.b: This judgment sees all the x in the table as solutions. Check again whether the column with value 3 satisfies f(x) < 0.
z-m-23-04.s.s1.o.c: 0, 1, 2, 3, and the integers outside the table are not solutions
z-m-23-04.s.s1.r.c: This judgment uses both the sign changes in the table and the shape of the quadratic function.
z-m-23-04.s.s1.o.d: The values can also be negative at integers outside the table, so it cannot be settled
z-m-23-04.s.s1.r.d: This judgment says that values not in the table are unknown. Think about what the conditions that it is a quadratic function and a > 0 tell you about outside the table.
z-m-23-04.s.s1.explain: f(−1) = 3 > 0 and f(0) = −1 < 0, so the sign changes between −1 and 0, and f(3) = −1 < 0 and f(4) = 3 > 0, so it changes between 3 and 4. For a quadratic function with a > 0, the x with f(x) < 0 form a single interval, so the solution is the inside between those two points, and the integers are 0, 1, 2, 3. (If you find the expression f(x) = x² − 3x − 1 and check, you get the same conclusion.)
z-m-23-04.s.s2.prompt: A student reasoned as below from the table above. Choose the wrong line, the claim that cannot be made from the table alone.
z-m-23-04.s.s2.hint.0: Distinguish whether each line says something from only the values written in the table or says something about values at x not in the table.
z-m-23-04.s.s2.hint.1: From the fact f(1) = f(2), write which x the graph is symmetric about, and compare the value at that x with the other values in the table.
z-m-23-04.s.s2.line.0: f(−1) = 3 > 0 and f(0) = −1 < 0, so the sign of the value of f changes between −1 and 0.
z-m-23-04.s.s2.line.1: f(3) = −1 < 0 and f(4) = 3 > 0, so the sign also changes between 3 and 4.
z-m-23-04.s.s2.line.2: For a quadratic function with a > 0, the x with values less than 0 form a single interval, so that interval lies between the two points above.
z-m-23-04.s.s2.line.3: Therefore the integers x with f(x) < 0 are 0, 1, 2, 3.
z-m-23-04.s.s2.line.4: Also, f(1) = f(2) = −3, so the minimum value of f is −3.
z-m-23-04.s.s2.explain: Line 5 is wrong. You cannot state the minimum value by looking only at the values at integers x. If f(1) = f(2), the axis of symmetry is x = 1.5 and the minimum occurs there. In this table, f(x) = x² − 3x − 1, so f(1.5) = −3.25, which is less than −3. Lines 1 to 4 can be stated correctly using only the table and the condition a > 0.
z-m-23-04.s.s3.prompt: If only the table above were given, without the condition "quadratic function with a > 0", could you settle that 0, 1, 2, 3 are the only integers with f(x) < 0? Write the reason and what information would be needed to settle it.
z-m-23-04.s.s3.hint.0: Assume the values can be anything between the integers x of the table (between 1 and 2) and outside the table (5 or more), and imagine cases where the integers with f(x) < 0 increase.
z-m-23-04.s.s3.hint.1: Look back at which judgments used the condition "quadratic function with a > 0" in the previous steps.
z-m-23-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: It cannot be settled. The table ... so ... is needed.
z-m-23-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write what differs between having the condition of being a quadratic function and not having it?
z-m-23-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you think specifically about what the values could be between table entries (between 1 and 2) or outside the table (5 or more, −2 or less)?
z-m-23-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write at least one piece of information needed to settle it?
z-m-23-04.s.s3.model.0: It cannot be settled. The table shows the values at only a few integers, so I do not know how the values change between 1 and 2 or outside the table (5 or more). Only with the condition that it is a quadratic function with a>0 can we say the interval where it is negative is a single interval.
z-m-23-04.s.s3.model.1: No. If it is not a quadratic function but another function passing through the points of the table, it could be negative at places like 5 or −2, and it could also rise to positive between 1 and 2. We can settle it only with the condition of being a quadratic function or more values outside the table.
z-m-23-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: It also gave values outside the table as additional information.

z-m-23-05.title: Why x + y = 6, xy = 8 has two pairs of solutions, and the case with one pair
z-m-23-05.topic: The number of solutions of symmetric simultaneous equations with a given sum and product
z-m-23-05.goal: Understand that in simultaneous equations where x and y play the same role the solutions come in ordered pairs, and the exception (x = y), and make an example with exactly one solution pair yourself.
z-m-23-05.material: In the following simultaneous equations, x and y are real numbers and solutions are counted as ordered pairs (x, y). "(2, 4)" means "x is 2, y is 4" and is a different ordered pair from (4, 2). The simultaneous equations: x + y = 6, xy = 8. We also think about the number of solutions of simultaneous equations of the form x + y = s, xy = p (s and p are integers) in general.
z-m-23-05.thinking.1: Finding a counterexample to a generalization
z-m-23-05.prereq.0: H1 in this task only marks the difficulty of this production category; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to high school grade 1. Assumed learning order: learners who have already learned quadratic equations, quadratic inequalities, and the relationship between roots and coefficients.
z-m-23-05.prereq.1: Practice with simultaneous quadratic equations that can be solved by plugging a linear expression into a quadratic expression
z-m-23-05.prereq.2: The meaning of an ordered pair ((2, 4) and (4, 2) are different ordered pairs)
z-m-23-05.prereq.3: The double root of a quadratic equation
z-m-23-05.s.s1.prompt: How many pairs of real ordered pairs (x, y) satisfy both x + y = 6 and xy = 8?
z-m-23-05.s.s1.hint.0: Plug in 2, 4, 3 for x one by one, choose y so that the sum is 6, and check whether the second equation xy = 8 holds.
z-m-23-05.s.s1.hint.1: Organize in a table whether (2, 4), (4, 2), and (2, 2) each satisfy both equations.
z-m-23-05.s.s1.r.a: This judgment counts the two ordered pairs with the values of x and y swapped as different solutions.
z-m-23-05.s.s1.o.b: 1 pair: (2, 4) and (4, 2) are the same solution
z-m-23-05.s.s1.r.b: (2, 4) means "x is 2, y is 4" and (4, 2) means "x is 4, y is 2". Check whether the values of x and y in the two equations are different.
z-m-23-05.s.s1.o.c: 4 pairs: plug 2 and 4 freely into x and y
z-m-23-05.s.s1.r.c: Plug (2, 2) and (4, 4) into the two equations and check whether the sum is 6.
z-m-23-05.s.s1.o.d: Cannot be determined: the equation about the product has infinitely many solutions
z-m-23-05.s.s1.r.d: Each equation by itself has infinitely many solutions, but how many pairs satisfy both equations at once has to be worked out separately.
z-m-23-05.s.s1.explain: Once x is determined, y is determined by the sum condition y = 6 − x, and from xy = 8, x(6 − x) = 8, that is, (x − 2)(x − 4) = 0. When x = 2, y = 4, and when x = 4, y = 2, so the ordered pairs are the two pairs (2, 4) and (4, 2). (2, 2) and (4, 4) do not have sum 6, so they are not solutions.
z-m-23-05.s.s2.prompt: Mina thought about the number of solutions of simultaneous equations of the form x + y = s, xy = p as follows. Which line is the first wrong one?
z-m-23-05.s.s2.hint.0: Plug (3, 3) from lines 3 and 4 into the two equations to check that it works, and then compare with the claim in lines 1 and 2.
z-m-23-05.s.s2.hint.1: Find out whether there are cases where (a, b) and (b, a), with the order swapped, are the same ordered pair, and what relationship between a and b makes this so.
z-m-23-05.s.s2.line.0: x + y = s, xy = p do not change even if x and y are swapped. So if (a, b) is a solution, (b, a) is also a solution.
z-m-23-05.s.s2.line.1: Therefore the solutions come only in pairs of (a, b) and (b, a), and the number of solutions is always even.
z-m-23-05.s.s2.line.2: For example, in x + y = 6, xy = 9, plugging y = 6 − x into xy = 9 gives x(6 − x) = 9, that is, (x − 3)² = 0.
z-m-23-05.s.s2.line.3: Then x = 3, y = 3, so the solution is the one pair (3, 3).
z-m-23-05.s.s2.line.4: It should be even but it is one pair, so the calculation in line 3 is wrong.
z-m-23-05.s.s2.explain: Line 2 is the first wrong one. (a, b) and (b, a) are the same ordered pair when a = b, so they do not form a pair. Line 3 was correctly calculated as (x − 3)² = 0, and (3, 3) satisfies both equations (3 + 3 = 6, 3 · 3 = 9). So the conclusion in line 5 is also wrong.
z-m-23-05.s.s3.prompt: For x + y = s, xy = p (s and p are integers), make 3 different simultaneous equations that have exactly one pair of real solutions (x, y). After making them, explain why there is only one pair.
z-m-23-05.s.s3.hint.0: If there is only one pair, (a, b) and (b, a), with the order swapped, must be the same pair. Write what relationship between a and b is needed.
z-m-23-05.s.s3.hint.1: Calculate the sum and product of x, y with that relationship (for example, x = y = 3) and decide s and p.
z-m-23-05.s.s3.fail.c1: Please take s and p to be integers.
z-m-23-05.s.s3.ok.c2: There is exactly one pair of solutions.
z-m-23-05.s.s3.fail.c2: There is not one pair of solutions. There are two pairs of real (x, y) satisfying both equations, or none at all.
z-m-23-05.s.s3.explain: If there is only one pair, x = y, so s = 2x, p = x², and s² = 4p. Examples: (s, p) = (2, 1) → (1, 1), (4, 4) → (2, 2), (−6, 9) → (−3, −3), (0, 0) → (0, 0). (6, 8) has two pairs, (2, 4) and (4, 2), and (2, 5) has no real solutions (only complex solutions). It is the same as saying the quadratic equation t² − st + p = 0 has a double root.
z-m-23-05.s.s3.because.prompt: Using the roles of x and y, explain why the simultaneous equations you just made have only one pair of solutions.
z-m-23-05.s.s3.because.hint.0: Write what the two equations become when x and y are swapped.
z-m-23-05.s.s3.because.hint.1: Write what relationship (a, b) and (b, a) have when there is only one pair of solutions.
z-m-23-05.s.s3.because.placeholder: Example: Even if we swap x and y, ... so ...
z-m-23-05.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write the condition under which (a, b) and (b, a) become the same?
z-m-23-05.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you check how the s and p you made connect to that condition?
z-m-23-05.s.s3.because.model.0: Even if we swap x and y, the equations stay the same, so if (a,b) is a solution, (b,a) is also a solution. For there to be only one pair, the two solutions must be the same, so the only case is a=b, that is, x=y.
z-m-23-05.s.s3.because.model.1: If the solution is (a, b), then (b, a), with the order swapped, is also a solution, so they usually come in pairs. For there to be only one pair, the two numbers must be the same, so only the case s=2x, p=x² works.
z-m-23-05.s.s3.because.modelNote.1: It connected all the way to the equations with s and p.

z-m-23-06.topic: Cases where a solution is missed in an equation with a common factor on both sides
z-m-23-06.goal: Understand why, in an equation where the same factor is multiplied on both sides, the case where that factor is 0 has to be checked separately, and pick out and make equations for which the solution method misses solutions and equations for which it does not.
z-m-23-06.material: A student solved the equation (x − 2)(x − 5) = 3(x − 2). x is a real number and the solutions are also limited to real numbers. (How to read: "x minus 2 times x minus 5 equals 3 times x minus 2".)
z-m-23-06.thinking.0: Finding the error in a solution
z-m-23-06.thinking.2: Making counterexamples (examples where a solution is missed) yourself
z-m-23-06.prereq.0: H1 in this task only marks the difficulty of this production category; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to high school grade 1. Assumed learning order: learners who have already learned quadratic equations, quadratic inequalities, and the relationship between roots and coefficients.
z-m-23-06.prereq.2: Checking a solution of an equation by plugging it into the original equation
z-m-23-06.prereq.3: The fact that you cannot divide by 0
z-m-23-06.s.s1.prompt: A student solved the equation (x − 2)(x − 5) = 3(x − 2) as below. Which line is the first one with a problem?
z-m-23-06.s.s1.line.0: Both sides of (x − 2)(x − 5) = 3(x − 2) are multiplied by (x − 2).
z-m-23-06.s.s1.line.1: Dividing both sides by (x − 2) gives x − 5 = 3.
z-m-23-06.s.s1.line.3: Plugging x = 8 into the original equation gives 6 · 3 = 18 and 3 · 6 = 18, so it holds.
z-m-23-06.s.s1.line.4: Therefore the only solution of this equation is x = 8.
z-m-23-06.s.s1.explain: A problem first appears in line 2. If x = 2, then x − 2 is 0, so it amounts to dividing by 0. If you plug x = 2 into the original equation, both sides are 0, so x = 2 is also a solution. The check in line 4 only shows that x = 8 is a solution and does not mean there are no other solutions. So "the only one" in line 5 is wrong, and the actual solutions are 2 and 8.
z-m-23-06.s.s2.prompt: The following equations all have the same factor (x − 1) multiplied on both sides. Which one loses no solution at all when solved by dividing both sides by (x − 1)?
z-m-23-06.s.s2.hint.0: Plug x = 1 directly into each equation and check whether both sides are equal.
z-m-23-06.s.s2.hint.1: For each equation, set the other two expressions left after removing (x − 1) equal and compare whether its solution is 1.
z-m-23-06.s.s2.explain: In all four equations, plugging in x = 1 makes both sides 0, so x = 1 is a solution. If the solution of the equation left after dividing is 1, no solution is missed. a gives 2 from x + 2 = 4, b gives −1 from 3 = x + 4, and c gives 5 from x − 3 = 2, so all of them miss x = 1. d gives x = 1 from x + 3 = 4, so no solution is missed, and since it is (x − 1)² = 0, the only solution is 1.
z-m-23-06.s.s3.prompt: In equations of the form (x − a)(x − b) = c(x − a) (a, b, c are integers from −9 to 9), make 3 different equations for which the solution method of dividing by (x − a) misses one solution. The same equation written differently (same a and same b + c) counts as the same example.
z-m-23-06.s.s3.hint.0: First choose an a and check that x = a is a solution of the original equation, then choose b and c so that the solution of x − b = c, obtained by setting the remaining factors equal, is different from a.
z-m-23-06.s.s3.hint.1: When making several (a, b, c), check that ones with the same a and only the same b + c are the same equation, and choose different a or b + c.
z-m-23-06.s.s3.fail.c1: Please take a, b, c to be integers.
z-m-23-06.s.s3.fail.c2: a, b, c must be from −9 to 9.
z-m-23-06.s.s3.ok.c3: x = a is a solution but it differs from the solution x = b + c of the remaining equation after dividing, so it is missed.
z-m-23-06.s.s3.fail.c3: x = a is the same as the solution b + c of the remaining equation after dividing, so no solution is missed.
z-m-23-06.s.s3.explain: (x − a)(x − b) = c(x − a) is (x − a)(x − b − c) = 0, so the solutions are x = a and x = b + c. The method of dividing gets only x = b + c. If a ≠ b + c, the solution a is missed. Examples: (a, b, c) = (2, 5, 3) → solutions 2 and 8, (1, 4, 0) → 1 and 4. For (2, −1, 3), b + c = 2 = a, so the only solution is 2 and nothing is missed.
z-m-23-06.s.s3.because.prompt: Explain what value the missed solution is and why this solution method cannot be used as it is at that value.
z-m-23-06.s.s3.because.hint.0: Write for what value of x the expression x − a is 0.
z-m-23-06.s.s3.because.hint.1: Write what each side becomes when you plug that x into the original equation.
z-m-23-06.s.s3.because.placeholder: Example: The missed solution is ... Because ...
z-m-23-06.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write exactly that the missed solution is x = a?
z-m-23-06.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you connect the fact that x − a is 0 at that value with "you cannot divide by 0"?
z-m-23-06.s.s3.because.model.0: The missed solution is x=a. If x=a, then x−a is 0 and we cannot divide by 0, so we have to check that case separately.
z-m-23-06.s.s3.because.model.1: The solution x=a, where the common factor x−a is 0, is a solution of the original equation, but the method divides by an expression that is 0 there, so this solution disappears. You have to plug that value into the original equation separately.
z-m-23-06.s.s3.because.modelNote.1: It also wrote the remedy of checking separately.
z-m-23-06.title: Solving (x − 2)(x − 5) = 3(x − 2) by dividing both sides
z-m-23-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write what calculation produced each line of the solution from the line before, and check whether that calculation can be used for every x.
z-m-23-06.s.s1.hint.1: When dividing, write what values the divisor must not be, and check whether that value is possible for x in this problem.
z-m-23-06.s.s2.r.a: This is a judgment that compared whether x = 1 is a solution and whether it is also among the solutions of the expression left after dividing.
z-m-23-06.s.s2.r.b: Put in x = 1 to see whether both sides are 0, and compare whether the solution of the expression left after dividing, x + 2 = 4, is 1.
z-m-23-06.s.s2.r.c: x = 1 is a solution, but the only solution of the expression left after dividing, 3 = x + 4, is −1.
z-m-23-06.s.s2.r.d: x = 1 is a solution, but the only solution of the expression left after dividing, x − 3 = 2, is 5.
